historical_timeline.summary: Pneumonia at about two years old; frail health thereafter.
First woman to win the Premier Grand Prix de Rome for composition, with Faust et Hélène.
Villa Medici in Rome; left for Nice when war broke out.
In Paris: headaches, loss of appetite, fever, and colitis-like symptoms; much of the time in bed, still composing.
With her sister, helped found the Franco-American Committee of the Conservatoire.
Second stay in Rome, then return to France.
Operation in Paris; later dictated her music to her sister.
Died at Mézy-sur-Seine; her illness described as intestinal tuberculosis and later proposed to be Crohn disease.

claims.statement: Lili Boulanger was born Marie-Juliette Olga Boulanger on August 21, 1893, in the 9th arrondissement of Paris.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Reference works give the given names in different orders (Juliette Marie Olga; Julie-Marie Olga); the national library's civil-register form is used.

claims.statement: She was a composer, the sister of the composer and teacher Nadia Boulanger (1887–1979).
At about two years old, in 1895, she had pneumonia, described as bronchial pneumonia; her health was frail from a very young age and she remained sickly for the rest of her life.
The usual account is that the childhood pneumonia left her immune system weakened, so that she never fully recovered.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A biographical interpretation, not a documented immune diagnosis; no test of her immunity exists.

source_links.locator: Describes low immunity, attributed to inflammatory bowel disease

claims.statement: In 1913, at 19, she became the first woman to win the Premier Grand Prix de Rome for musical composition, with the cantata Faust et Hélène; she had been the only woman among the five finalists that May.

She went to the Villa Medici in Rome in 1914. The outbreak of war made her leave Rome for Nice, where she composed the song cycle Clairières dans le ciel; she stayed in Rome again in 1916 and then returned to France.
claims.clinical_interpretation: One source says she instead made an unauthorized return to Paris in the summer of 1914; the record does not rely on either detail.

source_links.locator: Unauthorized return to Paris in summer 1914

claims.statement: Early in 1915, living in Paris, she began to have headaches, loss of appetite, and fever, followed by symptoms resembling colitis and appendicitis; she spent much of her time in bed but kept composing.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Reported in an encyclopedia article drawn from the Spycket biography, which was not read directly. The documented presentation that anchors the synthetic episode.

claims.statement: During the war she and her sister helped to found the Franco-American Committee of the Conservatoire, which kept mobilized students in touch with the Conservatoire.
Her chronic intestinal illness has been described as intestinal tuberculosis, and several reference works give tuberculosis as the cause of her death.
claims.clinical_interpretation: No test from her lifetime confirming tuberculosis is reported in the sources read; whether she had intestinal tuberculosis is not settled.

source_links.locator: Diagnosed at the time as intestinal tuberculosis

claims.statement: Later writers have proposed that her chronic intestinal illness was Crohn disease, which was not described as a distinct disease until well after her death.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A retrospective diagnosis in program notes, a music magazine, and an encyclopedia article; no peer-reviewed analysis was found. It conflicts with the tuberculosis account, and the cause of death is not settled.

source_links.locator: Intestinal tuberculosis, now known as Crohn's disease

claims.statement: After her return to Paris in 1917 she had an operation at the end of July; the operation and its findings are not named in the source read. In her last illness, unable to hold a pen, she dictated her music to her sister.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Later than the synthetic episode and not used in it.

claims.statement: She died on March 15, 1918, at Mézy-sur-Seine (Yvelines), at 24.
claims.clinical_interpretation: One reference biography places the death in Paris and another in the Paris area; the national library authority record gives Mézy-sur-Seine. Record the death as a fact without detail.

source_links.locator: Evacuated to a house in Mézy-sur-Seine

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Evaluate chronic abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss in a young woman of 21: confirm Crohn disease by ileocolonoscopy with biopsies and MR enterography, and exclude intestinal tuberculosis before any immunosuppression (interferon-gamma release assay, chest X-ray, and biopsies for acid-fast bacilli, TB PCR, and culture); classify the disease (Montreal) and its risk; start an advanced therapy early for moderate to severe disease, with latent tuberculosis, hepatitis B, and vaccine preparation first; correct iron, vitamin D, and nutrition; protect bone; treat to target with CRP, fecal calprotectin, and endoscopy; plan contraception, fertility, and pregnancy; screen mood; and help her keep composing. The historical illness is graded R: called intestinal tuberculosis in her time and proposed to be Crohn disease since, it is not settled.

problems.display: Crohn disease of the terminal ileum and colon (ileocolitis), Montreal A2 L3 B1 without perianal disease, moderate to severe: deep ileal ulcers over 15 cm and patchy colonic ulcers, SES-CD 14, Harvey-Bradshaw Index 11; intestinal tuberculosis excluded by negative interferon-gamma release assay, normal chest X-ray, and biopsies negative for acid-fast bacilli, TB PCR, and mycobacterial culture; synthetic modern diagnosis linked to her documented chronic intestinal illness, whose historical diagnosis is not settled

coding.display: Crohn's disease of both small and large intestine without complications

provenance.synthetic_reason: Synthetic diagnosis confirmed within the modern episode; her historical illness is documented (D), but whether it was intestinal tuberculosis or Crohn disease remains a retrospective interpretation (R) and is disputed.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Boulanger returns nine days after presenting with four months of right lower abdominal cramping, loose stools up to six times a day and at night, evening fevers, and loss of 6 kg. The ileocolonoscopy five days ago showed deep longitudinal ulcers over the last 15 cm of the terminal ileum and patchy ulcers in the ascending and transverse colon with normal mucosa between and a spared rectum (SES-CD 14). The biopsies show chronic active ileitis and colitis with crypt distortion and a few small non-caseating granulomas; the acid-fast stain and TB PCR are negative and the mycobacterial culture is pending. MR enterography two days ago shows 18 cm of inflamed terminal ileum without stricture, fistula, abscess, or necrotic nodes. The interferon-gamma release assay is negative and the chest X-ray normal. Stool tests for Clostridioides difficile, bacterial pathogens, and parasites are negative, and celiac serology is negative. The pregnancy test is negative. She has five or six loose stools a day with cramping and fatigue (Harvey-Bradshaw Index 11). She met Dr. Nwankwo-Delacroix this morning and chose a treatment with him. She has a concert of her choral works in late March and asked whether she could still perform.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Boulanger is a 21-year-old woman with ileocolonic Crohn disease, ten weeks into risankizumab and in clinical remission since the prednisone taper ended three weeks ago. Yesterday evening she developed sudden nausea and vomiting, six times overnight, then watery, non-bloody diarrhea eight times since, with cramping across the whole abdomen, aching, and a temperature of 37.8 °C at home. Two of her fellow musicians in the same rehearsal group were ill with the same symptoms this week. She has had no antibiotics. She is keeping down small sips. She wanted to know whether this was her Crohn disease returning and whether she should delay her next risankizumab dose.

referral.question: Suspected inflammatory bowel disease in a woman of 21 with four months of right lower abdominal pain, diarrhea, fevers, and weight loss, with iron deficiency anemia and a fecal calprotectin of 1240 ug/g. Ileocolonoscopy, MR enterography, and tuberculosis screening are being arranged. Please see her once they are done to confirm the diagnosis and plan treatment with her
referral.pertinent_history: Crampy right lower quadrant pain, loose stools up to six times a day including at night, evening temperatures to 37.6 °C, and loss of 6 kg over four months; frail health and a serious pneumonia in early childhood. On examination BMI 17.6, mild right lower quadrant tenderness, and a normal perianal examination. Hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL, MCV 76, ferritin 9, platelets 452, CRP 38 mg/L, albumin 3.3 g/dL, vitamin D 18 ng/mL, B12 normal. Never smoker; no regular medicines except acetaminophen; no known allergy. Not sexually active. She is a composer with a concert of her choral works in late March. Tuberculosis is an important alternative diagnosis, so no steroid has been started
questions: Do the endoscopic, histologic, and imaging findings confirm Crohn disease, and is intestinal tuberculosis adequately excluded?
How would you classify her disease and its risk of a disabling course?
Which advanced therapy do you recommend, and should a corticosteroid bridge be used?
What screening and vaccines are needed before immunosuppression?
How should her anemia, nutrition, and bone health be managed?
What are the treatment targets and the monitoring plan, and what should she know about fertility and pregnancy?

consultant_note.history: Ms. Boulanger is seen at the request of Dr. Marchetti-Rowe with four months of right lower abdominal cramping, five or six loose stools a day with one at night, evening fevers, fatigue, and loss of 6 kg. The ileocolonoscopy five days ago showed deep longitudinal ulcers over 15 cm of the terminal ileum and patchy ulcers in the ascending and transverse colon with a spared rectum (SES-CD 14); MR enterography showed 18 cm of inflamed terminal ileum without stricture, fistula, or abscess. She has no perianal, joint, eye, or skin symptoms. She has never smoked. She was told directly that the findings show Crohn disease, a lifelong condition that can be controlled, and asked to hear the treatment choices with their trade-offs
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Ileocolonoscopy images and report; biopsy histology with acid-fast stain and TB PCR (mycobacterial culture pending); MR enterography; chest X-ray; interferon-gamma release assay; hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV, measles, and varicella serology; stool tests and celiac serology; blood counts, iron studies, CRP, albumin, vitamin D, and fecal calprotectin; Dr. Marchetti-Rowe's referral

exam.finding: Two small aphthous ulcers inside the lower lip
Tender in the right lower quadrant with fullness but no discrete mass
No fistula, abscess, or skin tags

assessment.display: Crohn disease of the terminal ileum and colon, Montreal A2 L3 B1, moderate to severe
assessment.assessment: Long ileal ulcers, skip lesions, a spared rectum, small non-caseating granulomas, and the MR findings confirm Crohn disease. Intestinal tuberculosis can look the same; against it here are a negative interferon-gamma release assay, a normal chest X-ray, no caseating or confluent granulomas, no necrotic nodes, and negative acid-fast stain and TB PCR. That is enough to start treatment, but the mycobacterial culture must be checked when final. Diagnosis before 30, extensive deep ulcers, and weight loss predict a disabling course, so she should start an advanced therapy now

Options discussed with her: infliximab with azathioprine, adalimumab, ustekinumab, risankizumab, and vedolizumab. She chose risankizumab: effective for induction and maintenance in ileocolonic disease, given as three infusions and then a home injection every eight weeks, without an added immunomodulator and with a low rate of serious infection. The trade-off she accepted is that data in pregnancy are more limited than for anti-TNF drugs. A short prednisone bridge will control symptoms until risankizumab acts

Tuberculosis screen negative. Hepatitis B surface antigen and core antibody negative, but surface antibody below 10 after an infant series: a booster is advised. Immune to measles and varicella, so no live vaccine is needed and treatment need not wait

Iron deficiency from blood loss and inflammation is best treated intravenously. Moderate malnutrition needs dietitian support. Vitamin D deficiency, low weight, and a steroid course call for vitamin D, calcium during the steroid, and a baseline DXA

The targets are clinical response early, steroid-free remission and a normal CRP by about week 12, a normal fecal calprotectin by about six months, and endoscopic healing at six to twelve months. Crohn disease in remission does not reduce fertility; the main risk to a pregnancy is active disease, so a pregnancy should be planned in remission
